symptom: fact_repayment_behavior declared grain 'one row per customer_id' did not hold: 47,180 rows carried a NULL customer_id. dbt's `unique` test passed anyway.
root_cause: Unmatched home_credit xwalk rows resolve to a NULL customer_id (R-29 late-arriving dimension). SQL `UNIQUE` semantics treat NULLs as distinct, so dbt's generic `unique` test excludes them from the assertion entirely — the test cannot see a NULL-key grain violation by construction.
fix: Commit 9e5eb19. Grain enforced explicitly rather than relying on dbt `unique`; 3 poisoned Silver prefixes deleted from S3 (see INC-0002); re-verified against S3 and live Snowflake: 287,530 rows / 0 NULL customer_id / 0 duplicates.
lesson: A passing uniqueness test does not prove key integrity when NULL semantics are involved. Assert NOT NULL on the key separately — `unique` and `not_null` test different things and only their conjunction expresses a grain.

symptom: Corrected upstream logic could not retract already-written Silver rows; three Silver prefixes stayed poisoned until deleted manually from S3.
root_cause: merge_upsert issues whenMatchedUpdateAll + whenNotMatchedInsertAll only — it has no delete branch by design (D-06 soft-delete semantics; hard-delete replay deferred to Fasa C per R-25). A row written by a previous, defective run is therefore never retracted by a corrected run: re-running Silver cannot heal rows whose keys are no longer produced. Operationally remediated by deleting the 3 prefixes from S3; the underlying no-delete property is unchanged, so this is diagnosed, not fixed.
lesson: An upsert-only writer makes bad rows permanent. Recovery from a defective run needs an explicit retraction path (delete-and-recreate, or tombstones); re-running is not a recovery strategy on its own.

symptom: Three 'one row per key' selections could return a different survivor on a re-run of identical input: merge_upsert (orderBy(lit(1))), latest_state_from_cdc_log (groupBy+first after orderBy), latest_balance_per_account (orderBy(date) with same-day ties). No error, correct row counts.
root_cause: None of the three orderings was a total order, so row_number()/first() resolved ties by executor/partition order, which is not part of the query semantics. Spark documents first() as non-deterministic because a shuffle may change row order — and groupBy shuffles, discarding the preceding orderBy.
fix: pipeline/common/ordering.py::latest_row_per_key — ordering always closes with a content-derived tie-break (sha2 of the row struct), so the survivor is stable across runs, partition counts and cluster sizes. All three call sites now use it. Regression tests: tests/test_cdc_ordering_determinism.py (10 tests).
lesson: 'Stable per run' is not 'deterministic across runs'. A dedup whose row count is right can still pick a different row each time, and nothing reports it.

symptom: MYR conversion computed amount.cast('double') * rate_to_myr with rate_to_myr stored as DoubleType, making any SUM over the converted column dependent on partition order.
root_cause: IEEE-754 addition is not associative. Spark chooses the addition grouping by partitioning, so a float monetary SUM is order-dependent. The error is confined to low digits and never raises, so it presents as irreproducible totals rather than a failure.
fix: pipeline/common/money.py — MONEY=DECIMAL(18,2), FX_RATE=DECIMAL(18,6); to_myr and dim_fx_rate converted to fixed point end to end. Regression tests: tests/test_money_precision.py (11 tests). Precision/scale assumptions documented in money.py, as no journey/ or ADR document specifies them.
lesson: Money must be fixed-point. A float total that changes between two runs of identical input is an audit finding, not a rounding preference.

symptom: INC-0004 was recorded as fixing the money path 'end to end', but fixed point held only in the middle of it. Silver still cast every Berka and OBP monetary column to double, so the representation error was baked in BEFORE Gold converted; and the Snowflake serving layer re-declared amount, amount_myr, current_balance, current_balance_myr and rate_to_myr as DOUBLE, so every dbt mart aggregate (sum(amount_myr), sum(current_balance_myr), approx_percentile) is float-summed again AFTER Gold. Nothing raised at any point.
root_cause: The fix was applied at the layer where the defect was observed (to_myr) rather than across the path the value travels. Gold's own cast to DECIMAL(18,2) actively hid the Silver half: rounding a double back to 2dp recovers ordinary amounts, so the output looked correct and only degrades at large magnitudes. journey/05_STTM.md had declared these Silver columns 'decimal' the whole time, so the double casts were already a violation of a locked contract that no gate checked.
fix: Silver half FIXED: pipeline/silver/silver_core_banking.py:57 and pipeline/silver/silver_crm.py:158-159 now use pipeline/common/money.py::to_money (DECIMAL(18,2)), casting from the source representation rather than via double. Boundary guard added at pipeline/gold/common.py::to_myr (assert_no_float_money) so a float monetary column fails closed instead of rounding quietly. Regression tests: tests/test_money_precision.py::TestMoneyPathHasNoFloatReentry (2 static guards, mutation-verified to fail when either defect is reintroduced). Serving half NOT FIXED: snowflake_setup.sql still declares the monetary virtual columns DOUBLE — that is a consumer-facing contract change (Power BI reads it) and is left for owner decision, not changed unilaterally. mart_daily_flows.py:37's double-cast net_flow is in a file RETIRED from orchestration (dbt owns the marts), so it is recorded, not fixed.
lesson: A fix belongs to a data path, not to the file where the symptom was noticed. Trace the value from source to consumer and check both ends — a downstream cast that ROUNDS a bad value is not a fix, it is camouflage.
